about.title: About
about.intro: I'm a senior backend developer and technical lead, working mostly with C# and .NET. I design and modernize enterprise systems, and I lead a team of five developers while staying hands-on in architecture and code.

journey.title: How I got here
journey.text: I started as a full-stack developer maintaining legacy enterprise applications. Over the years I moved into backend architecture for a new platform and, later, into technical leadership. Working with both legacy and modern code shaped how I decide: I weigh business continuity, scalability and maintainability together.

craft.title: Development and leadership
craft.text: I favor Clean Architecture and SOLID because they keep systems easy to change, and I pick tools for the problem at hand. As a technical lead, I review code, mentor developers and help define the engineering standards the team works by.

ai.title: Exploring AI
ai.text: I'm studying AI systems development and management, and I use study projects to explore LLMs, AI agents, RAG and prompt engineering, with a focus on validating what the models produce. They are learning projects, and I present them that way in the AI Lab.

metadata.title: Football Stat Analytics | Bruno Lucildo
metadata.description: An academic project that analyzes football athlete performance with AI, retrieval and layered answer verification: architecture, technical decisions and current state.

football.overview: Football Stat Analytics is a command-line application that analyzes football athlete performance with AI. It indexes scouting reports, answers questions grounded in those reports and offers an interactive chat with analyst personas. It is an academic project.
football.challenge: Language models readily produce statements that sound right but have no support: invented numbers, actions the data never mentioned and flattering adjectives. In sports analysis that is worse than no answer. The challenge was to keep every answer tied to the evidence the user supplies or to the reports that were indexed.
football.solution: Answers pass through layers of checking. Deterministic rules enforce the output format and reject unsupported numbers and wording. A semantic verifier, a second model that must quote the evidence, judges each statement. A failed answer gets one automatic correction attempt, and answers based on reports end with a grounding report showing what could be traced back to the retrieved excerpts.
football.architecture: The application is written in TypeScript on Node.js, using native type stripping and the built-in SQLite module. Ingestion extracts text from PDF reports, translates it, splits it into chunks, generates embeddings with the OpenAI API and stores them in SQLite. Retrieval ranks chunks by a hybrid score that combines embedding similarity and keyword overlap, and sends the five best to the answer prompt. The chat keeps its session history in SQLite and summarizes older messages when the context grows. The code separates AI behavior (personas, policies, validation and verification) from storage and retrieval, and 109 automated tests cover it with stubbed model calls, so they run without an API key.

decisions.title: Rules in code, not only in prompts.
decisions.text: Prompt instructions alone cannot guarantee that the model follows a policy, so the most important rules are checked by code.

decisions.title: A judge that is not trusted blindly.
decisions.text: The verifier must quote the evidence, and a quote that is not in the evidence is rejected. If the verifier itself fails, the chat keeps working and shows a warning.

decisions.title: Optional consensus, off by default.
decisions.text: Answering with the median of three samples costs three times the generation and did not make the scores reliably stable, so it is available but disabled.

decisions.title: Simple local storage.
decisions.text: Conversation history and embeddings live in SQLite files, which keeps the project easy to run and inspect.

football.state: In development. The project describes itself as experimental: answers are not checked against official statistics, PDF ingestion does not run OCR, and the checks are safeguards that do not replace human review. A known limitation is retrieval: the index has no athlete metadata to filter on, so a question about one athlete can retrieve excerpts about others.

metadata.title: Reelix | Bruno Lucildo
metadata.description: A personal movie and series tracking app with privacy-first sharing and spoiler control: architecture, technical decisions and current state.

reelix.overview: Reelix is an app to discover and track movies and series, record what you have watched and share authorized activity with friends. The repository holds a React Native mobile app and an ASP.NET Core API. It is a personal project.
reelix.challenge: A viewing diary is personal data. Sharing it with friends only works if each person controls what is shared, and comments and ratings must not spoil a plot for someone who has not watched yet. The challenge was to build social features on top of that, with privacy and spoiler control as rules of the product rather than afterthoughts.
reelix.solution: Sharing is opt-in and split into separate consents for history, ratings and favorites. Comments are private by default, can be flagged as spoilers and stay hidden until the reader chooses to reveal them. Progress tracking, lists, achievements and a monthly ranking among friends are built on the same rules.
reelix.architecture: The API is a modular monolith in ASP.NET Core (.NET 10), organized in Domain, Application, Infrastructure and Api projects so that business rules do not depend on frameworks or the database. Data lives in PostgreSQL through Entity Framework Core. Supabase Auth handles sign-in, and the API validates its tokens and maps them to the internal account. Movie and series metadata comes from TMDB, behind an adapter, with provider credentials kept on the server. The mobile app uses React Native with Expo, strict TypeScript, Expo Router and TanStack Query. A GitHub Actions workflow runs the backend tests, the mobile lint and type checks, dependency audits and secret scanning.

decisions.title: A modular monolith before microservices.
decisions.text: The design stays simple until real usage justifies more infrastructure.

decisions.title: One identity system.
decisions.text: Supabase Auth is the only provider, and a second system such as ASP.NET Identity was deliberately not added.

decisions.title: Providers behind an adapter.
decisions.text: The catalog integration can be replaced without touching business rules, and provider keys never reach the app.

decisions.title: AI kept off until decided.
decisions.text: An automatic spoiler classifier exists on the server but is disabled by default while cost and data policy are decided; manual spoiler flagging works without it.

reelix.state: In development. The code covers accounts, onboarding, discovery, tracking, lists, ratings and comments, friends, notifications and achievements, but the repository itself states that this describes the implementation and does not confirm a production deployment. Remote push notifications are disabled, the Android widget is not implemented and the mobile app has no automated tests yet.
